description_ru: Поход по маршруту W в Торрес-дель-Пайне: ветер, срывающий шляпы, ледники синего цвета и рассвет на гранитных башнях.
text:
Nobody tells you that the wind in Patagonia has a personality. On the first afternoon of the W trek in Torres del Paine, I was standing on a ridge above Lake Nordenskjöld, admiring a view that looked as if it had been painted by an enthusiastic child with an unlimited supply of turquoise, when a gust came out of the west and removed my hat. It did not blow it away so much as confiscate it. The hat rose, hovered for an instant, and departed across the valley with a dignity I could only envy.

The trek is called the W because of the shape of its route on the map: three long valleys, each running into the mountains, linked by two stretches along the shores of lakes. It covers around eighty kilometres and takes four or five days, which, as the guidebooks like to say, is manageable for anyone of reasonable fitness. The guidebooks are correct, with the proviso that none of them has attempted to walk into a thirty-knot headwind carrying a pack. In the park, where gusts regularly exceed a hundred kilometres an hour, the day can be less a hike than a negotiation.

On the second morning, I set off for the French Valley under a sky of unbroken grey. The trail climbs gently through forests of lenga, a type of southern beech whose twisted trunks are draped with lichen, and then crosses a hanging glacier's long moraine. At one point, I stopped to drink from a stream and heard, high above me, a sound like distant artillery. It was an avalanche of ice, tumbling from the hanging glacier on the mountain called Paine Grande. The noise rolled around the amphitheatre for what felt like a minute. A woman nearby, a retired surgeon from Zürich, murmured, "Magnificent, and thoroughly indifferent to us," which seemed to me exactly right.

The summit of the valley, a natural amphitheatre ringed with granite spires, looks like a cathedral built by a geologist. The towering dark horns, called the Cuernos, are especially curious: their pale granite bases are capped by dark sedimentary rock, laid down on an ancient sea floor and lifted, tilted and carved over millions of years. It is a rare chance to see, in a single glance, a record of deep time. I sat on a boulder, unwrapped a squashed sandwich, and was happy.

Wildlife appears when you stop looking for it. Herds of guanacos, the wild relatives of the llama, grazed beside the trail and watched me pass with the languid disdain of aristocrats. On the pass above the lake, a pair of Andean condors rode the updraught without once flapping their wings, and I counted the span of one against the width of the valley, a ridiculous exercise that left me more impressed rather than less. A tiny red fox appeared at the door of the refugio each evening, and each evening a guide told us, with weary patience, not to feed it.

The accommodation is a story of its own. Along the route, a chain of refugios offer bunk beds, hot dinners and, crucially, walls. I stayed in one where thirty strangers shared a single long dining room, and over lentil stew and a very reasonable Carménère, the room acquired the atmosphere of a slightly damp reunion. A pair of Chilean students taught me the rules of a card game whose logic I never fully grasped. A Dutch couple, who had been walking for two weeks, compared blisters with the earnest pride of veterans. By nine o'clock, everyone had fallen asleep, and the only sound was the wind, still trying to find a way in.

On the third day, I walked to Grey Glacier, a tongue of ice that descends from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field, one of the largest expanses of ice anywhere outside the polar regions. Standing at the viewpoint, I watched small icebergs drift in the lake, some of them a shade of blue so intense that it seemed almost artificial. The colour, I was reminded, arises because dense ice absorbs the red end of the spectrum and scatters blue. Yet the glacier is retreating. Park guides, who speak of it without drama, mark its edge each year. The old photographs in the refugio show an icy front that reached far closer to the shore.

The final morning belonged to the Torres themselves, three vertical towers of granite that give the park its name. To see them at dawn, you must climb in the dark, scrambling up a boulder field by headtorch, so that you arrive at the lake beneath the towers before sunrise. I did. For an hour, the sky remained a leaden grey, and the crowd of hikers around me shivered and muttered. Then, abruptly, a thin band of light broke through to the east, and the granite caught fire. The towers flushed from pink to orange to a burning, impossible gold, and everyone, as one, stopped talking.

I have thought a great deal about why that moment affected me. Part of it, I suspect, was fatigue, the way four days of effort strip away your usual cynicism. But part of it was simply scale, the sense that the world was made on a larger plan than I had remembered, and that I was a small, windblown, dependent creature in the middle of it.

I did not find the hat. Somebody in the refugio told me that it would turn up eventually, perhaps in Argentina, wearing sunglasses. I have decided to believe that.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Ударение: ˈamphitheatre (в американском), sediˈmentary, faˈtigue. В sedimentary ударение на -men-.
Служебные слова the, that, there: звонкое «ð», язык чуть между зубами.
Конечное -ing — носовой «ŋ»: walking, standing. Не добавляйте «г» после «н».
«w»: губы вытянуты вперёд, как при «у»: wind, west, walk. Не «в».

questions.question: Why is the trek called the W?
questions.answer: Its route on the map has the shape of a W.

questions.question: What happened to the writer's hat?
questions.answer: The wind took it and it was never found.

questions.question: Why does the ice at Grey Glacier look so blue?
questions.answer: Dense ice absorbs red light and scatters blue.

questions.question: What happens at dawn at the Torres towers?
questions.answer: The granite catches light and turns pink, orange and gold.
